The robe, sandals, the beard and hair were made of gold. He wore a silver olive wreath on his head. The throne was made of gold, bronze, ebony, ivory, and gems. It was decorated with scenes from mythology. This Zeus was the kindly Zeus rather than the fierce and powerful Zeus. The Roman emperor Caligula wanted the statue sent to Rome. He planned to take the head off and replace it with an image of his own. The statue does not survive. It was probably shipped to Constantinople about 393 AD and destroyed in a fire there in 475 AD. The statue was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.

The Temple of Artemis ( or Latin: Artemisium), was a temple dedicated to the goddess Artemis. It was also known as the Temple of Diana (Diana was a Roman goddess). It was completed around 350 BC at Ephesus (in present-day Turkey). The area was under the Achaemenid dynasty of the Persian Empire, but some of its cities were Greek. Only ruins of the temple remain. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The Temple of Artemis was near the ancient city of Ephesus, about 50 km south from the modern port city of İzmir, in Turkey. Most of the description of the Temple of Artemis comes from Pliny, though there are different accounts that give different sizes. Pliny said the temple was 115 meters long and 55 meters wide. He said it was made almost completely of marble. It was about three times as big as the Parthenon by area. The Temple has 127 Ionic-styled columns. Each is 17.5 meters in height. The Temple of Artemis had many fine artworks. Bronze sculptures by famous Greek sculptors Polyclitus, Pheidias, Cresilas, and Phradmon were in the temple. Paintings and gilded columns of gold and silver were also in it. The sculptors often competed at creating the best sculpture. Many of these sculptures were of Amazons, who are said to have founded the city of Ephesus. Pliny said that Scopas, who also worked on the Mausoleum of Mausollos, worked carved reliefs into the temple's columns. Athenagoras of Athens names Endoeus, a student of Daedalus, as the sculptor of the main statue of Artemis in Ephesus. The Temple of Artemis was at a flourishing region. It was used as a religious institute. Merchants and travellers came to it from all over Asia Minor. The temple was influenced by many beliefs. It can be seen as a symbol of faith for many different peoples. The Ephesians worshiped Cybele. They joined many of their beliefs into the worship of Artemis. Artemisian Cybele became very different from the Roman goddess Diana. The cult of Artemis attracted thousands of worshipers from far-off lands. They all gathered at the site and worshipped her.

Literature is a group of works of art that are made of words. Most are written, but some are shared by word of mouth. Literature usually means a work of poetry, theatre or narrative. There are many different kinds of literature, such as poetry, plays, or novels. They can also be put into groups by their language, historical time, place of origin, genre, and subject. The word "literature" comes from the Latin word "literatura," which means "writing formed with letters." Most of the earliest works were epic poems. Epic poems are long stories or myths about adventures, such as the Epic of Gilgamesh from ancient Mesopotamia. Ramayana and Mahabharta, two Indian epics, are still read today. The Iliad and Odyssey are two famous Greek poems by Homer. They were shared over time through speaking and memory and were written down around the 9th or 8th century BCE. Literature can also mean imaginative or creative writing, which is read for its artistic value. Literature is also related to people and community. According to Sangidu (2004) as quoted by Arfani et.al (2023), "literature is a part of society, a fact that inspires authors to involve themselves in the life order of the community where they are and try to fight for the position of the social structure and the problems face in society".

Egyptian literature is some of the earliest known literature. The Egyptians were the first culture to develop the book. The ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus. They also wrote on walls, tombs, pyramids, obelisks, and more. A well-known example of ancient Egyptian literature is the Story of Sinuhe; Alexandria became an important center of early Christianity from around the 1st to 4th century CE. Writing by Coptic Christians was important to Christian literature at that time.The Nag Hammadi library protected some books from being lost or destroyed. Muslim Arabs controlled Egypt by the eighth century. Libraries and literature were important in Arab Egypt. Several important changes for writers happened at this time. Cloth paper replaced papyrus. Writers began using calligraphy. Also, writers began to write mostly about Islam. The earliest novel written in Egypt was Ibn al-Nafis' Theologus Autodidactus. It was an early science fiction and religious novel. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the Arab world experienced a cultural change like the Renaissance. This was called al-Nahda movement. It touched nearly all areas of life, including literature. One of the most important people from this time was Naguib Mahfouz. He was first Egyptian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Another important modern writer was Muhammad Husayn Haykal. He wrote Zaynab in 1914. It is an Islamic novel and is called the first modern Egyptian novel.

The term English literature means literature written in the English language. English is a language known by many millions of people. They can read literary works from any country in an English translation. English literature began in Old English with the epic poem Beowulf, which dates from sometime between the 8th to the 11th centuries. It is not written in language people can understand today, but there are several good translations into modern English. It is the most famous work in Old English, despite being set in Scandinavia. The poem is written with no rhymes but with alliteration. The next important landmark is the works of the poet Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400), especially The Canterbury Tales. That is in Middle English, from 1066 to the middle/late 1400s. Chaucer introduced into English poetry rhyme royal, which is a seven-line stanza rhymed ababbcc. Modern English literature began in the 16th century. Thomas Wyatt and Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey wrote the first English sonnets. Howard also invented blank verse. Edmund Spenser wrote The Faerie Queene, a long epic poem, while Philip Sidney wrote a sequence of sonnets Astrophel and Stella. The next stage is Thomas Kyd, Christopher Marlowe, Ben Jonson, William Shakespeare and John Milton, sometimes described as Early Modern English (1470 to 1650). Shakespeare is the author of the most famous sentence written in English: To be, or not to be, that is the question. It is the first line of Prince Hamlet's monologue from drama The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark that was published in 1603. The King James Version of the Bible was published in 1611. John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress which is one of the most popular books ever published. In the 18th century, the first modern novels were written by Daniel Defoe, Jonathan Swift, Laurence Sterne and Horace Walpole. William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, John Keats,Jane Austen, Emily Brontë, Charles Dickens, Robert Browning, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, D.H. Lawrence, Virginia Woolf and Ted Hughes are all important English writers in modern English. T.S. Eliot was perhaps the most important poet in 20th century who wrote in English. His best known work is the poem The Waste Land that was published in 1922. Another book by him was The Four Quartets. The poet himself regarded it as his best work. Not all English literature was written by writers born in England. English literature includes all the varieties and dialects of English spoken around the world. Joseph Conrad was Polish, Robert Burns was Scottish, James Joyce was Irish, Dylan Thomas was Welsh, Edgar Allan Poe was American, Hilaire Belloc was French, Emma Lazarus was Jewish, Salman Rushdie is Indian, V. S. Naipaul is Trinidadian, and Vladimir Nabokov was Russian. The greatest Portuguese poet of the 20th century, Fernando Pessoa wrote some poems in English, too. American literature is poetry, fiction, drama, or essays written by Americans. It also includes literature written by people living in the United States (who are not American citizens). The 19th century was a fertile era for the American novel and American poetry. The most popular American novelists of the 19th Century were women. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin about slavery in America. Luisa May Alcott wrote the popular novel Little Women about the dreams and hardships of sisters growing up in rural America. Herman Melville wrote the famous novel Moby Dick, about a whaling in America. Moby Dick is often called the greatest American novels. Emily Dickinson is one of the greatest American poets. Dickinson wrote many lyrical, religious, philosophical poems. Walt Whitman wrote the epic poem Leaves of Grass. Masterpieces of Gothic fiction include Nathaniel Hawthorn's Fall of the House of Usher and The Scarlet Letter). Charlotte Perkins Gilman's feminist classic "The Yellow Wallpaper" is also Gothic fiction. Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau wrote philosophical essays. Their philosophical school of thought is called Transcendentalism. The 20th Century is often called The American Century in art. Novelists of the modern era include William Faulkner, John Steinbeck, T.S. Eliot, Ernest Hemingway, Sinclair Lewis, and Pearl Buck. Toni Morrison, Eugene O'Neill, Saul Bellow, Joseph Brodsky and Isaac Bashevis Singer won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Contemporary fiction writers of include Don Delillo, Paul Auster, Jennifer Egan, Colson Whitehead, Giannina Braschi, David Foster Wallace, and Jonathan Frazen. These writers are often called Postmodern authors. There are many popular literary genres. Humorist David Sedaris writes funny short stories about his personal life and odd things about strangers. Shel Silverstein and Dr.Seuss wrote rhyming poems for children’s books. Judy Bloom writes emotional stories about young girls for young readers. R.L.Stine writes scary stories (Goosebump Series) about monsters and ghosts for boys and girls. Stephen King writes horror novels for adults about murder, monsters, and kidnapping.

Australian literature is literature made by Australians or people who live in Australia. In Australia's early history, it was made of many British colonies. So, it is in some ways similar to British literature. Common themes in Australian literature are friendship, equality, democracy, and Australian cultural identity. Some Australian book writers are Marcus Clarke, Miles Franklin, Patrick White, Thomas Keneally, Morris West and Colleen McCullough. Some bush poets are Henry Lawson and Banjo Paterson. Some historians are Manning Clark and Geoffrey Blainey. A playwright is David Williamson. Some writers who were born in Australia, but moved somewhere else, are Barry Humphries, Robert Hughes, Clive James and Germaine Greer.

Canadian literature is literature written in Canada, or by Canadians. Notable writers include Charles Sangster, Saul Bellow, Margaret Atwood, Mordecai Richler, Michael Ondaatje and Alice Munro. French Canadian literature is literature written by French Canadians.

French literature is literature written in the French language. Much of it comes from France, but much also comes from other places where people speak French. These places include Belgium, Switzerland, Quebec, Haiti, Senegal, and the countries of North Africa. Literature written in French outside France is often called francophone literature. French literature has a history of about 1,200 years. The first known words in French were written in the 9th century. Long poems about war and love appeared in the 11th and 12th centuries. Printing came in the 15th century. After this, books slowly became available to more readers. French literature has had a strong influence on other countries. French writers helped to develop the essay, the modern novel about society, Symbolism in poetry, Surrealism, and the Theatre of the Absurd. Literature has a very important place in public life in France. Writers often speak in public about politics and society. Newspapers and television often report on books, literary prizes, and writers. Schools also spend many hours studying both old and modern French texts. French developed from Latin, the language of the Roman Empire. It is one of the Romance languages, together with Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese. It also has words from Celtic languages and from the Germanic language of the Franks. For a long time, there was no single form of French. In the north, people spoke different forms of the langue d'oïl. In the south, they spoke the langue d'oc, which is now called Occitan. Writers usually used the language of their own region. Some of the oldest poetry from the area that is now France is in Occitan rather than French. Many modern histories of French literature include this poetry. They also include writing in French from countries outside France, instead of treating it as less important. The forms of French used around Paris, at the royal court, and in government offices slowly became the basis of standard French. In 1539, King Francis I signed the order of Villers-Cotterêts. After this, French had to be used in the law courts instead of Latin. A rule for law courts is not the same as the language spoken by ordinary people. Most people living inside the borders of modern France did not speak French as their first language until the end of the 19th century. At that time, education became free and required by law. Breton, Basque, forms of Occitan such as Gascon and Provençal, and Alsatian were still used in daily life. The Académie française began as a private group. From about 1629, nine men met each week in the Paris house of Valentin Conrart, a secretary of the king, to talk about news, business, and books. People called them purists, because they wanted to keep the language pure. Cardinal Richelieu heard about the group in the first months of 1634. He offered it his protection, and the members understood that they could not refuse. The group became an official body and took in powerful men, until it had forty members. Louis XIII signed its charter on 25 January 1635. However, the Paris parlement feared that the new body would become a tool of the government. It did not register the charter until 10 July 1637, and it added that the Academy could deal only with the French language. Richelieu controlled every election, and he used the members to correct his own speeches. The members of the Académie had to protect the French language and prepare a dictionary. The idea that the language needs rules and careful protection has remained strong in France ever since. The first surviving text written in a form of French is not a poem. In 842, two grandsons of Charlemagne met at Strasbourg and swore an oath there. Part of the text was written in the language spoken by their soldiers. These Oaths of Strasbourg are the oldest surviving written evidence of French. The first surviving poem in French came a little later. The Sequence of Saint Eulalia, written around 880 or 881, has only 29 lines. It tells how a young Christian woman chose death rather than give up her faith. Other early religious works include the Passion of Christ, the Life of Saint Leger, and the Life of Saint Alexis. These early works show that religion played an important part in the birth of written literature in French. The south had its own early works in Occitan. They include the Boeci, a poem about Boethius written around 1030, and the Song of Saint Faith, written later in the 11th century. After the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, Anglo-Norman French also became an important literary language. Latin remained the main language of the Church, schools, learning, and official writing. But clerics began to use the languages spoken by ordinary people when they wanted to reach a wider public. The growth of French literature was therefore also the story of a spoken language slowly becoming a language that could be used for books. Most people in the Middle Ages could not read for themselves. However, this does not mean that literature belonged only to an oral world. A text could be written in a manuscript and then read, recited, or sung to people who could not read it. Written and spoken literature worked together. From the 12th century, written texts also became more important as sources of knowledge and authority. This helps to explain why so much medieval literature is in verse. Rhythm, repeated sounds, and music were useful in performance, but verse was also a respected literary form. Many poems were written down even when they were meant to be heard. Books were copied by hand. Two copies of the same work could therefore be quite different. A writer or copyist might shorten a story, add new parts, change its language, or join it to another story. Medieval readers often enjoyed hearing old material told again in a new way. Modern scholars call this process remaniement, or reworking. For this reason, the modern idea of a book with one author and one final text does not always fit medieval literature. Many works are anonymous, and some survive in several different forms. Other writers, however, did give their names. Wace, Marie de France, Chrétien de Troyes, Jean Bodel, Rutebeuf, and many later poets clearly present themselves as writers. During the 14th and 15th centuries, authors became even more visible in their own books. A chanson de geste was a long poem about war, brave actions, families, kings, and loyalty. The name means "song of deeds". Many of these poems were performed by people called jongleurs. A jongleur could sing, tell stories, play music, or entertain an audience in other ways. A poet and a performer were not always the same person. The poems are made of laisses, which are groups of lines without a fixed length. Most lines have ten or twelve syllables, although some early poems use shorter lines. The oldest chansons de geste usually do not rhyme. Instead, the lines of one laisse end with the same main vowel sound. This is called assonance. Rhyme became more common later. Repetition is very important. A scene may be told more than once with small changes. The same words and groups of words come back again and again. These effects gave the poem a strong sound when it was spoken or sung. About 120 chansons de geste survive. Their stories usually take place in the time of Charlemagne or his son Louis. They deal with war, loyalty to a lord, family honour, Christian faith, and conflict between powerful men. By the end of the 12th century, writers were already placing these poems into large families or cycles. One group told of Charlemagne and his family. Another told of Guillaume d'Orange and his relatives. A third group told of barons who fought against their king. The most famous chanson de geste is La Chanson de Roland. The oldest complete version is kept at Oxford and has a little over 4,000 lines. The manuscript was made in the 12th century, but scholars cannot give the poem itself one exact date. The story comes from a real event in 778. Roland, one of Charlemagne's military leaders, died when part of the emperor's army was attacked in the Pyrenees, at the pass of Roncevaux. In the poem, this small defeat becomes a great Christian war. Roland dies as a heroic warrior, Charlemagne takes revenge, and the traitor Ganelon is punished. There is no single fixed Roland. Other medieval versions change the poem and make it much longer. Other important chansons de geste include The Song of William, The Crowning of Louis, The Cart of Nîmes, The Taking of Orange, Aliscans, Raoul of Cambrai, The Four Sons of Aymon, Huon of Bordeaux, and The Song of Antioch. These poems were not simple records of French history. They changed the past to speak about the needs and ideals of their own time. Much later, readers also used them to imagine a heroic national past. Around 1100, a new kind of poetry appeared in the south. Its poets are called troubadours, and they wrote in Occitan. The first troubadour whose name is known is Guilhem IX, duke of Aquitaine. Eleven songs are attributed to him. Some are love songs, while others are comic or openly sexual. The word troubadour is linked to the Occitan verb trobar, which means to find or create. A troubadour made poetry and usually its music as well. A jongleur was more often the person who performed the work, although one person could sometimes be both poet and performer. The most famous subject of troubadour poetry is fin'amor, often called courtly love. In many songs, the poet presents himself as the faithful servant of a lady whom he cannot easily have. He must be patient, loyal, and controlled. Love should improve him. This poetry is highly formal. The speaker's feelings should not always be read as a private diary. The poet works with known ideas, situations, rhyme patterns, and melodies, and tries to make something new from them. Love was not the only subject. The canso was usually a love song. A sirventes could attack an enemy or speak about politics and war. A crusade song asked knights to fight in the Holy Land or spoke of the pain caused by leaving home. In an alba, or dawn song, two lovers have to separate when morning comes. A pastourelle usually tells of a meeting between a knight and a shepherd girl. Important troubadours include Jaufre Rudel, Marcabru, Bernart de Ventadorn, Arnaut Daniel, Bertran de Born, Guiraut de Bornelh, Peire Vidal, Peire Cardenal, and Raimbaut de Vaqueiras. Dante later praised Arnaut Daniel and learned from the art of the troubadours. In northern France, similar poets were called trouvères. Their poetry developed mainly during the 12th and 13th centuries. Famous trouvères include Gace Brulé, Conon de Béthune, the Châtelain de Coucy, Thibaut de Champagne, Colin Muset, and Adam de la Halle. Their songs survive in large manuscript collections called chansonniers. The town of Arras became an especially important centre. Noblemen, rich townsmen, clerics, and professional performers all took part in its literary life. Poets met in societies called puys, where songs could be performed and judged. Some poets also moved away from the normal language of courtly love. Rutebeuf, who lived in 13th-century Paris, wrote about poverty, bad luck, friendship, religion, politics, and the university. His poems often sound very personal, although they also use literary roles and conventions. The word romance did not first mean a love story. The Old French word romanz meant the spoken Romance language, especially French, instead of Latin. A work translated or written in this language could be called a romanz. The word slowly became the name of a kind of long story. Some of the first romances retold stories from the ancient world. The Roman de Thèbes, the Roman d'Enéas, and Benoît de Sainte-Maure's Roman de Troie turned Greek and Roman stories into works for a medieval audience. Their ancient heroes often behave like medieval knights. These works are sometimes called the "Matter of Rome". Another group of stories came from Britain. Around 1155, Wace wrote the Roman de Brut, based on Geoffrey of Monmouth's history of the kings of Britain. His work helped to make King Arthur and his court important subjects in French literature. Marie de France also drew on stories connected with Brittany and Britain. Her short verse tales, called lais, tell of love, marriage, strange adventures, fairies, werewolves, and suffering. Their small size does not make them simple: they often ask difficult questions about love, loyalty, and freedom. The stories of Tristan and Iseult were also very popular. Tristan and Iseult drink a love drink and are unable to stop loving each other, even though Iseult is married to King Mark. The poems of Béroul and Thomas survive only in parts. The story was later made into a very long prose romance. Chrétien de Troyes was the greatest writer of Arthurian romance in the 12th century. Five of his romances survive: Erec and Enide, Cligès, Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, Yvain, the Knight of the Lion, and Perceval, the Story of the Grail. Chrétien did not simply copy old stories. He says that a writer must give his material a good order or conjointure. His heroes go on adventures, but the adventures test more than physical courage. A knight must learn how to balance love, honour, duty, and life with other people. Chrétien probably used both spoken tales and written books. Wace's Brut was one important written source. The mixture of different sources is typical of medieval writing. Perceval introduced the Grail into surviving literature. Chrétien left the work unfinished. Other writers then continued it, adding tens of thousands of lines. The Grail story also changed. In later texts, it became much more clearly Christian. During the 13th century, writers increasingly used prose for Arthurian stories. The great cycle now called the Lancelot-Grail joins the history of Arthur, the love of Lancelot and Guinevere, the search for the Grail, and the fall of Arthur's kingdom into one very large story. These French stories travelled across Europe. They were translated, rewritten, and joined to local traditions. Centuries later, they were still one of the main sources for Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur in England. Allegory became one of the most important ways of writing in the Middle Ages. An allegorical story gives human form to ideas, feelings, or moral qualities. A writer can therefore make Love, Fear, Reason, Fortune, or Death speak and act like people. The most famous example is Le Roman de la Rose. Guillaume de Lorris began it around 1230. His part tells a dream in which a young man enters a garden and tries to reach a rose. The rose stands for the woman he loves. Feelings and ideas such as Love, Shame, Fear, and Hope become characters. Jean de Meun continued the poem about forty years later. His continuation is much longer and very different. Characters give long speeches about love, nature, money, marriage, women, society, religion, and political power. The poem can be comic, satirical, learned, and deliberately difficult. Le Roman de la Rose became one of the most widely read French books of the later Middle Ages. It influenced poetry, dream stories, and allegorical writing for centuries. It also caused an important literary argument. Around 1401 and 1402, Christine de Pizan criticised Jean de Meun, especially his treatment of women and love. Jean de Montreuil and the brothers Gontier and Pierre Col defended the poem. Jean Gerson later supported Christine. This "Quarrel of the Rose" is one of the first large public debates in French about the value and moral meaning of a literary work. Religious writing did not disappear when romances and love poetry became popular. It remained one of the largest parts of medieval literature. Writers continued to make lives of saints, prayers, sermons, Bible stories, and poems about death, sin, and salvation. The cult of the Virgin Mary produced many works. In the early 13th century, Gautier de Coinci wrote his large collection of Miracles de Notre-Dame. It contains nearly sixty stories as well as songs and other poems. His language can be playful and technically difficult, and he also uses the stories to attack faults in society. Preachers often used short examples called exempla. An exemplum was a small story that helped to explain a moral or religious lesson. Collections of such stories grew during the 13th century. Some of the same stories also entered fabliaux, animal stories, and other forms of short fiction. French also became a language for teaching about the world. Writers made bestiaries about animals, lapidaries about stones, books of moral teaching, and encyclopedic works. Gautier de Metz's Image du monde explained the structure of the universe. Brunetto Latini, an Italian scholar, wrote his large encyclopedia Li Livres dou Trésor in French. Translation became more important as well. In the 14th century, King Charles V supported translations of major Latin works into French. Writers such as Nicolas Oresme helped to make subjects that had once belonged mainly to Latin learning available in French. Medieval literature was therefore not only a literature of knights, love, and adventure. It was also used to teach religion, history, science, good behaviour, and ways of understanding the world. Medieval literature could also be comic, rude, and openly critical of society. The fabliaux are short verse stories, mostly from the 12th and 13th centuries. Many are anonymous. They tell of cheating husbands and wives, hungry priests, clever peasants, foolish townsmen, thieves, sexual tricks, and arguments about money. Their humour can be very coarse. They often turn the normal social order upside down: the weak person wins, the clever person defeats the powerful one, and respected people are made to look foolish. The Roman de Renart is another large comic tradition. It is not one novel written by one author. It is a group of stories, or "branches", written by different people. Renart the fox tricks his enemy Isengrin the wolf and many other animals. Noble the lion is a king, and his court looks very much like a human royal court. These works can tell us something about medieval towns, trades, food, money, marriage, law, and social tensions. However, they are not simple pictures of everyday life. Their characters are types, and their world is often changed by exaggeration, parody, and satire. The beginnings of medieval theatre are difficult to explain. Older histories often said that French theatre grew directly out of church services. Modern scholars are more careful. Religious ceremony was important, but there were probably several different paths from performance to written drama. The oldest surviving play in French is the Jeu d'Adam, written in Anglo-Norman in the 12th century. It tells the stories of Adam and Eve and Cain and Abel. The French dialogue is mixed with Latin church texts. The manuscript also gives instructions for movement, costumes, objects, and sound. Around 1200, Jean Bodel of Arras wrote the Jeu de saint Nicolas. The story is religious, but the play also contains soldiers, thieves, drinkers, and scenes in a tavern. The sacred and the comic exist side by side. Rutebeuf wrote the Miracle de Théophile in the 13th century. Its hero gives his soul to the Devil and is later saved by the Virgin Mary. The same story became one of the most famous examples of the power of Mary's help. Arras was also the home of Adam de la Halle. His Jeu de la feuillée, written around 1276, makes fun of the poet himself and of people in the town. His Jeu de Robin et Marion combines dialogue and music. Drama became much larger during the 14th and 15th centuries. Miracles showed a saint or the Virgin saving someone in danger. Mysteries told large parts of the Bible or the life of a saint. Moralities used allegorical figures such as Good, Evil, or Death to teach a lesson. The largest mysteries could take several days to perform. Town governments, religious groups, and local people helped to prepare them. They used many actors, costumes, painted scenery, machines, and special effects. Arnoul Gréban's Mystère de la Passion, written around 1450, has more than 34,000 lines. Comic theatre grew beside religious theatre. A farce is usually short and fast, with tricks, arguments, and physical comedy. The most famous is La Farce de Maître Pathelin, written in the 15th century. A lawyer first cheats a cloth seller, but a shepherd later cheats the lawyer himself. The play became very popular. Medieval writers had already told history in verse. Wace wrote about the kings of Britain and the dukes of Normandy, while Benoît de Sainte-Maure wrote a large history of the Norman dukes. During the 13th century, however, French prose became increasingly important for historical writing. Geoffroi de Villehardouin was one of the leaders of the Fourth Crusade. He wrote about the events that ended with the capture of Constantinople in 1204. He explains and often defends the decisions of the crusade's leaders. Robert de Clari, a poorer knight from Picardy, wrote about many of the same events from a different social position. The two books are among the earliest important works of history in French prose. Jean de Joinville later wrote about Louis IX, or Saint Louis. He had known the king and had gone on crusade with him. His Life of Saint Louis, completed in 1309, mixes history, memory, religious teaching, and many small personal stories. Jean Froissart wrote four large books of Chroniques about the Hundred Years' War and the political world of the 14th century. He travelled widely and collected stories from people who had taken part in events. His descriptions of battles, journeys, ceremonies, and conversations often have the colour of a romance. Near the end of the Middle Ages, Philippe de Commynes wrote his Mémoires. He had served both Charles the Bold of Burgundy and Louis XI of France. He was less interested in heroic battles than in explaining why rulers made decisions and why political plans succeeded or failed. His book is part memoir, part political analysis, and part advice for rulers. Poetry changed greatly during the 14th century. Music and poetry did not suddenly separate, but poets increasingly wrote texts that could also exist on the page without a melody. Fixed forms became especially important. The main ones were the ballade, the rondeau, and the virelai. A ballade usually has three main stanzas. The same line returns at the end of each one as a refrain. Many ballades also have a short final part called an envoi. A rondeau repeats words from its beginning later in the poem. These forms gave poets strict rules, but they also allowed great technical variety. Guillaume de Machaut, who lived from about 1300 to 1377, was both a poet and a major composer. He wrote love poetry, narrative poems, religious music, and songs in fixed forms. He also took unusual care over the arrangement of his works in manuscripts. Machaut often makes "Guillaume" a character in his own narrative poems. This does not mean that every event is autobiography. It shows a new interest in the writer's own voice and in the act of making a book. Eustache Deschamps wrote thousands of poems. In 1392 he completed the Art de dictier, the first French treatise devoted to the art of verse. He called poetry a "natural music", different from the "artificial music" made with instruments. The subjects of poetry also became wider. Love remained important, but poets wrote more often about politics, war, disease, old age, the passing of time, and death. The long wars and the plague gave these subjects special force. Poets such as Deschamps repeatedly ask where the people and pleasures of the past have gone. Alain Chartier's La Belle Dame sans mercy, written in 1424, tells of a woman who refuses to love a suffering man. The poem caused another literary argument. Other poets wrote answers, attacks, and defences, showing how literature itself had become the subject of public debate. Christine de Pizan was born in Venice in 1364 but grew up in France. After her husband died, she built a career as a writer and worked for important patrons. She wrote lyric poetry, political works, moral teaching, history, and books about women. She took part in the debate about Le Roman de la Rose. In The Book of the City of Ladies, written in 1405, she imagines a city built from the lives of famous and worthy women. She argues against the idea that women are naturally less intelligent or less moral than men. Christine also wrote about the political troubles of France. Near the end of her life, she wrote the Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, celebrating Joan of Arc after the lifting of the siege of Orléans. Her career shows how strongly the position of the writer had changed since the anonymous literature of the early Middle Ages. Charles d'Orléans was a prince as well as a poet. He was captured at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415 and remained in England for about twenty-five years. Much of his poetry was written during this long captivity. His ballades and rondeaux speak about love, memory, sadness, age, time, and the seasons. Their language can be simple and quiet, although the poems are often carefully built around allegorical figures such as Love, Hope, or Melancholy. After his return to France, Charles kept a literary court at Blois where poets wrote answers to one another and competed in verse. François Villon was born around 1431 as François de Montcorbier. Guillaume de Villon, a churchman in Paris, helped to educate him. Villon studied at the University of Paris and became a master of arts in 1452. His later life is known mainly from legal records. He killed a man during a fight in 1455, took part in a robbery, and was imprisoned more than once. In 1463 he was sentenced to death after another street fight. The sentence was changed to ten years of banishment from Paris. After this, he disappears from the surviving records. His two main works are the Lais, written in 1456, and the much longer Testament, written around 1461. Both pretend to be legal wills. Villon gives strange or useless gifts to friends, enemies, officials, and people he knew in Paris. The poems move quickly between jokes and serious subjects. Villon writes about hunger, prison, sex, lost youth, old age, the body, and death. His voice can sound unusually direct, but the "Villon" inside the poems is also a carefully made literary character. Later readers often treated him as the first "modern" French poet because his voice seems so personal. Yet his work also depends deeply on medieval forms, university culture, satire, ballades, and the traditional poetry of death. At the same time, other kinds of literature flourished at the court of Burgundy. It produced the comic prose tales of the Cent Nouvelles nouvelles. Poets later called the Grands Rhétoriqueurs developed an art based on difficult rhyme, word play, and complex poetic forms. For most of the Middle Ages, books had to be copied by hand. This began to change in the second half of the 15th century. The first printing press in Paris was set up at the Sorbonne in 1470. Printing began in Lyon a few years later. The change was not immediate. Manuscripts and printed books existed together for a long time. Printers also chose many medieval works because readers already knew and liked them. Villon's works were printed in Paris in 1489. La Farce de Maître Pathelin also entered print near the end of the century. Old romances, chansons de geste, religious books, and collections of stories continued to be copied, rewritten, and printed. For this reason, there is no sharp line between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. Some new ideas and new ways of making books appeared during the 15th century, while many medieval forms continued into the 16th. French literature changed slowly, by keeping old traditions and giving them new forms. During the 16th century, French writers studied the writers of ancient Greece and Rome and the new literature of Italy. Scholars studied Greek and Hebrew as well as Latin. They wanted to read old books in the original languages used by their writers. This movement is called humanism. Humanists believed that studying old texts could make people wiser and better. They also believed that languages other than Latin could be used to express serious ideas. Printing helped to spread these ideas, but the change was slow. In 1528, only about one book in five printed in France was written in French. Most of the writers of the century came from the towns, from families of merchants and royal officials, from Marot and Rabelais to Calvin and Louise Labé. Lyon, the capital of banking, was also one of the capitals of poetry. Most of the others were in Latin or Greek. French did not make up more than half of new book titles until around the middle of the century. At the same time, the Christian church was dividing. The Protestant Reformation reached France during the 1520s. Many writers had to choose between the two sides, and some had to leave the country. The reformer Jean Calvin published a French version of his Institution de la religion chrétienne in 1541. He attacked the layers of commentary that tradition had piled on the text of the Bible. Giraud and Jung note that the new faith spread through the printed Bible in French. Lefèvre d'Étaples translated the New Testament in 1523, and Olivétan's complete Bible of 1535 became the Bible of French Protestants. In the night of 17 October 1534, posters attacking the Catholic mass were put up in Paris and other towns. Francis I treated this as a plot against the state, and from then on the religious question was also a political one. Clément Marot, who lived from 1496 to 1544, was the main French poet of the first half of the century. He wrote light and clever poems, letters in verse, and songs. He also translated psalms into French, and this caused trouble for him with the church. In 1536, while Marot was in exile at Ferrara in Italy, the poet François Sagon attacked him in a furious pamphlet. The quarrel that followed drew in many other poets. In Lyon, a group of poets wrote a more difficult kind of love poetry. Maurice Scève wrote long groups of short, dark, and carefully made poems. Two women from the same city, Pernette du Guillet and Louise Labé, also wrote about love. Their poems speak about women's own feelings and desires, rather than only showing women as the objects of men's desire. This was unusual at the time. Scève loved the poet Pernette du Guillet, who married another man. Giraud and Jung say that he had nothing left but to make his love live in poetry: Délie appeared in 1544, and Pernette died the following year. Labé's book of 1555 contains three elegies, twenty-four love sonnets, and a prose debate between Love and Folly. In 2006, a scholar argued that the real Louise Labé did not write these works. According to this view, a group of men around Scève wrote them. Scholars still disagree about this question. Around 1550, a group of young poets in Paris decided to make French poetry as great as poetry in Latin and Greek. This group became known as the Pléiade. In 1549, Joachim du Bellay published their plan in La Deffence et illustration de la langue françoyse. He said that French was not naturally a poor language. It seemed poor because writers had not worked enough to develop it. Poets should study ancient writers, create new words, and use the great forms of poetry. Pierre de Ronsard, who lived from 1524 to 1585, was the leader of the group. He wrote odes, sonnets, hymns, and an unfinished long poem about the beginnings of France. His love poems are still read, especially those about time, age, love, and flowers. Du Bellay is best remembered for Les Regrets. He wrote this book during four unhappy years in Rome. Its sonnets are simple, sad, and full of longing for home. The Pléiade also changed the form of French verse. Their first sonnets used lines of ten syllables. Ronsard began to write lines of twelve syllables around 1554, and Du Bellay used them throughout Les Regrets. This twelve-syllable line, called the alexandrine, became the main form used for serious French poetry during the following century. The group also brought tragedy on the ancient model to France: Étienne Jodelle's Cléopâtre captive was performed in 1553. François Rabelais, who was born in 1483 or 1494 and died in 1553, was first a monk and later a doctor. He did not invent the giants in his books. Gargantua already appeared in a cheap book of popular stories printed in 1532. Rabelais answered it in the same year with Pantagruel. He later wrote Gargantua and two more books. The search for the Holy Bottle, which ends the story, takes up the old search for the Grail in a comic form. The last of these appeared in 1552. A fifth book was published in 1564, eleven years after his death. Scholars still disagree about how much of it Rabelais wrote. The books are long and full of lists, jokes, and new words. Rabelais makes fun of bad teachers, greedy lawyers, foolish soldiers, and narrow-minded priests. Rabelais also uses comedy to discuss serious ideas. He wanted education to train both the body and the mind. He wanted people to think for themselves instead of only repeating old lessons. The group of religious teachers at the University of Paris, known as the Sorbonne, condemned his books. Although the king had granted him a privilege in 1545, the third book was condemned all the same, and Rabelais had to take refuge for some months at Metz, which was then outside France. Rabelais continued to write. He is now one of the best-known French writers. The word rabelaisian is still used for wild and physical comedy. Marguerite de Navarre, who lived from 1492 to 1549, was the sister of King Francis I. She protected writers who were in danger, including Rabelais and Marot. She wrote poems and plays, as well as a book of short stories called L'Heptaméron. In the book, five women and five men are stopped by a flood and tell stories to one another. The work follows the example of Boccaccio, but the storytellers promise to tell only stories that they know to be true. French readers already knew another book with the same kind of structure, the Cent Nouvelles nouvelles, which was put together at the court of Burgundy around 1460. Marguerite died before she could finish the book. She seems to have planned one hundred stories but left only about seventy. The book was first printed in 1558, nine years after her death. The stories are about love, marriage, violence, and religious faith. After each story, the people in the group discuss its meaning. The speakers often disagree. The book does not always tell the reader which answer is right. Michel de Montaigne, who lived from 1533 to 1592, was a judge at the court of Bordeaux. In 1571, when he was thirty-eight, he left this job and went to live in a tower with his books. There he wrote his Essais. Other writers had written short and personal pieces before him, but he gave them their name and made the form an important kind of writing. The French word essai means an attempt or a try. Montaigne wrote short pieces about many different subjects, including friendship, thumbs, sleep, cannibals, fear, books, and his own kidney stones. His method was to study himself. He said that he was the subject of his own book. He changes his mind and sometimes repeats himself. The reader can see how his ideas change as he writes. Montaigne did not remain alone in his tower. The first part of the Essais was published in 1580. He was mayor of Bordeaux from 1581 to 1585, and he continued adding to his book until his death. Montaigne lived during the wars of religion, when Catholics and Protestants killed one another in France. He supported the moderate side. During this time of violence, he wrote about doubt, self-control, and the right to think freely. The wars also produced a great Protestant poem, Les Tragiques by Agrippa d'Aubigné, which was printed only in 1616. It shows the recent history of France as a stage on which God judges the persecutors. The essay became one of the main forms of European writing. English writers began using it very quickly, and Shakespeare read Montaigne in translation. In the 17th century, France became the strongest country in Europe. Under Louis XIV, the king had almost all political power. French literature also changed. Writers followed more rules, and literature became more closely connected with the royal court and public life. The historian Jean Rohou divides the century into five periods. Until about 1625, poetry was the main form. From 1628 to 1642, under Richelieu, writers accepted discipline and the theatre grew. From 1643 to 1659 came comic poems, long novels, and the fashion of the précieuses. Rohou keeps the name classical only for the years from 1666 to 1678. After 1682, a period of criticism prepared the 18th century. He sees the whole century as a time of centralisation. The king, the capital, reason, and the rules of art all helped to bring French life under central control. Writers needed money. Few of them could live only from the sale of their books. They therefore looked for a rich protector or for money from the king. In return, they often praised the person who supported them. At the beginning of the century, the great noble families, such as the Condés and the Montmorencys, kept writers in their service. The historian Antoine Adam says that this saved writers from poverty, but at the price of their freedom. An important place for literature and good taste was the salon. A salon was a regular meeting held in the home of a woman from a rich or important family. Guests read new works aloud, played games with words, and discussed the French language. Moncondhuy says that the salons produced a new model of the social person, the honnête homme. He was a man of good manners and moderate learning who was at ease in company. The chevalier de Méré wrote about this ideal. He asked the honnête homme to look at his own life as if it were a play in which he was acting a part. The most famous early salon met in the Hôtel de Rambouillet in Paris. The Marquise de Rambouillet, who was born in Rome, had drawn the plans of the house herself. After seven births, her health was poor, and she could no longer go out. She therefore brought society into her own home. The influence of her salon on literature became strong around 1630. Its guests wanted above all to enjoy themselves. They organised parties and plays, and they played games with poems. In 1633 and 1634, the poets of the house wrote a set of short poems about flowers for the daughter of the marquise. It is known as the Guirlande de Julie. The poet Chapelain praised the salon because people spoke reasonably there, without showing off their learning. The grammarian Vaugelas, one of the first members of the Académie, observed the best usage of the language there rather than at the court. He later put his observations into a book of remarks on the French language. Later, the salon of Madeleine de Scudéry became known for its careful study of human feelings. From 1653, her friends met every Saturday in the Marais district of Paris. These meetings were called the samedis. The word précieuse appeared in Paris at the beginning of 1654. At first it meant a woman who was careful about love and who did not want to behave like a flirt. According to Adam, the précieuses protested against the way that marriages were arranged and against the way that custom treated women. They also attacked the learned men whom they called pedants. Their enemies made fun of them, and Molière did so in Les Précieuses ridicules (1659). The strange language that later writers gave them was largely invented by a satirist named Somaize in 1660. All the same, the salons did serious work. They helped to make the language clearer, removed many coarse words, and asked writers to express themselves clearly. The poet François de Malherbe (1555–1628) helped to bring about this change. He came to Paris in 1605, when he was already fifty years old. King Henry IV liked his poems and kept him at court. Malherbe gathered young poets in his home almost every day. He read their verses and showed them their faults. He rejected almost all the poetry of Ronsard. He wanted a poem to be clearly thought out, without rare words, old words, or difficult references. He also made strict rules about rhyme and about the shape of each stanza. He said that the porters of the Paris hay market were his masters for language. Adam explains that this only meant that a poet must use living words. In fact, Malherbe's real models were the court and the salons. His ideas helped to create the literary style now called classicism. A good work should be clear, well ordered, and true to nature. It should teach the reader as well as give pleasure. Personal feelings were less important than a form that everyone could understand and judge. In the theatre, these ideas became strict rules. The three unities required a play to have one main action, take place in one place, and happen within one day. Another rule was called bienséance, or proper behaviour. It kept violence and coarse language off the stage. Deaths usually happened away from the stage and were then described by a messenger. The Académie française gave official support to these rules. When Pierre Corneille did not fully follow them in Le Cid, the Academy was asked to judge the play. The 17th century was also a time of new ideas and difficult questions. René Descartes (1596–1650) was educated by the Jesuits at the college of La Flèche. He travelled through Europe as a soldier, and at the end of 1628 he settled in Holland. He lived there for most of his working life, and he died in Sweden. He published his Discours de la méthode in 1637. He wrote it in French instead of Latin so that more people could read it. He decided to doubt everything until he found one thing that he could not doubt: he was thinking, and therefore he existed. Adam sees his work as an answer to the sceptics who followed Montaigne. Descartes wanted to prove that human reason could reach certain truth and could guide human conduct. Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was born in Clermont. His father, who was himself a mathematician, taught him at home, and he never went to school. He spent two years building a calculating machine, which was ready in 1644. It was sold for one hundred livres, but it cost much more to make. In 1646, he repeated the experiments of the Italian scientist Torricelli on the weight of the air. He became close to the Jansenists, a strict Catholic group based at the abbey of Port-Royal. The Jansenists were strongly attacked by the Jesuits. In 1654, after some months of deep unhappiness, Pascal had a religious experience during the night of 23 November. It lasted about two hours, and he wrote an account of it that is now called the Mémorial. In January 1656, the Sorbonne was about to condemn the Jansenist leader Antoine Arnauld. Pascal wrote a short letter for the public. It was printed without any name and was only eight pages long. It was so successful that seventeen more letters followed. They are known as the Provinciales. Pascal used clear reasoning and jokes to attack the moral teaching of the Jesuits. Pascal died in August 1662 before he could finish his defence of the Christian faith. He had begun to work on it seriously in 1658. He wrote his notes on large sheets of paper, cut them into pieces, and tied some of them into 27 bundles. Most of the notes were never sorted. They were published in 1670 as the Pensées. They are short, direct, and sometimes frightening. Pascal writes about the silence of the endless universe and about how small human life is. Other writers followed a different path. The libertins were free thinkers who doubted religion. They usually expressed their ideas carefully because openly rejecting religion could be dangerous. The danger was real. The philosopher Vanini was burned at Toulouse in 1619, and the poet Claude Le Petit was executed in Paris in 1662. Théophile de Viau, the most gifted poet among the free thinkers of the 1620s, was kept in prison from 1623 to 1625. Theatre was the main public art of the 17th century. Paris had only a small number of theatres. Actors were popular with the public, but the Church often treated acting as sinful. Pierre Corneille (1606–1684) was born in Rouen. He studied with the Jesuits and became a lawyer. He wrote his first play, a comedy, in 1629 for a travelling company that visited the town. Le Cid was first performed in Paris in the first days of January 1637. Corneille called it a tragi-comedy, a kind of play with a happy ending that was popular at the time. In the play, a young man must kill the father of the woman he loves in order to defend the honour of his own father. She then asks the king for his death, although she still loves him. Adam says that the play was new because its characters had a will of their own. They chose their actions instead of being carried along by adventures. The play was a great success. It was performed three times at the Louvre in the following month, and Corneille's father received a title of nobility. However, the play also caused a long argument. Corneille answered his critics with pride, and other playwrights attacked him. One of them, Georges de Scudéry, said that the play broke the rules taken from Aristotle and asked the Académie française to judge it. Richelieu wanted the Academy to play this role. Its judgement, the Sentiments de l'Académie sur Le Cid, appeared at the end of 1637. It praised many details of the play but blamed its general plan. Corneille then wrote three tragedies on Roman subjects: Horace (1640), Cinna (1640–1641), and Polyeucte (1641–1642). Adam sees a progression in them. In Horace, love of country wins over family feeling. In Cinna, the emperor Augustus forgives the men who plotted against him, so that humanity wins over the interest of the state. In Polyeucte, a Christian martyr places God above all human feelings. Corneille often wrote about will and duty. His heroes choose the difficult path because they believe it is right, and they are admired for their strength. Molière (1622–1673), whose real name was Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was the son of a Paris upholsterer who worked for the king. He studied law but chose the theatre. In June 1643, with the actress Madeleine Béjart and her family, he founded a company called the Illustre Théâtre. It failed, he was put in prison for debt, and for thirteen years he toured the provinces with his actors. In October 1658, the company played before the young king in the Louvre. A short farce pleased the court so much that Louis XIV gave Molière the use of a theatre in Paris, the Petit-Bourbon, which he shared with an Italian company. He wrote comedies for the company and often played the main roles himself. Rohou points out that in his own time he was above all three things: a comic actor, a writer of satire, and the organiser of comedies with music and dance for the court. From 1664 to 1671, he was the main organiser of the king's entertainments. Molière often wrote about people who are controlled by one strong idea or fault. Tartuffe is about a man who pretends to be very religious. L'Avare is about a miser, a person who hates spending money. Le Misanthrope is about a man who cannot accept the lies of polite society. Les Femmes savantes makes fun of people who use learning mainly to impress others. His laughter attacks the power of masters over servants, of parents over children, of tyrannical husbands, of doctors, and of religious and learned pedants. However, it never touches the political order. Molière played the first three acts of Tartuffe at Versailles on 12 May 1664, during the festivities that opened the new palace. A group of religious people had already met to obtain its suppression. The play was banned for five years because religious groups said that it attacked religion itself. Molière answered that he was attacking only false religion. In his later plays, according to Rohou, the dangerous subjects of religion and politics gave way to the family. Harpagon, Monsieur Jourdain, and Argan are tyrants of their own households, and their madness is turned into joyful spectacle. On 17 February 1673, Molière felt ill during a performance of Le Malade imaginaire and died at home a few hours later. Two priests refused to come to him. Because the Church treated actors as sinners, the parish refused to bury him. His wife appealed to the king, who obtained a burial at night, without ceremony. Seven or eight hundred people followed the coffin by torchlight. Jean Racine (1639–1699) was born at La Ferté-Milon. His mother died when he was one year old and his father when he was three. The nuns of Port-Royal took in the poor orphan, and the teachers of the abbey educated him. He learned Greek there so well that he could read Homer and Plato with ease. In Paris, he made his name with the tragedy Alexandre at the end of 1665. Molière's company had staged it, but Racine secretly gave the play to a rival theatre. This broke his relations with Molière. A month later, he attacked his old teachers of Port-Royal in a public letter, because one of them had called writers of plays public poisoners. Racine wrote some of the most carefully built tragedies in French literature. He followed the rules of classical theatre very closely and used them as a strength. His plays usually have few characters and very little physical action. Most of the action happens inside the minds of the characters. In Andromaque (1667), Britannicus (1669), and Phèdre (1677), people are destroyed by a love that they did not choose and cannot control. His plays often show a view of human beings close to that of the Jansenists: people are weak and cannot easily save themselves. Phèdre was attacked by a group of enemies at court. Moncondhuy calls it the most purely tragic play of the whole century. In the same year, Racine married, made his peace with Port-Royal, and was named historian of the king together with Boileau. The king ordered the two men to leave everything else and write his history. Racine, who was 37 years old, stopped writing for the public theatre. Later, he wrote two religious plays, Esther (1689) and Athalie (1691), for a girls' school at Saint-Cyr. Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) published the first collection of his Fables on 31 March 1668. It contained 126 fables in six books, and it was dedicated to the king's son, who was seven years old. He took most of his stories from older writers. At first, he used mainly the Latin poet Phaedrus, in a school edition published by the Jansenists. Later he turned to Aesop and to Italian and Indian collections. Five more books appeared in 1678 and 1679, and a last book in 1694. This last book was dedicated to the young Duke of Burgundy, the son of the prince who had received the first collection. His special skill was the way he told these stories. The length of his lines changes to follow the movement of the speaking voice. His animals often speak like people from his own time: a proud lion who acts like a king, a fox who gives false praise, and a poor donkey who is blamed for everything. The later books were dedicated to Madame de Montespan, the king's mistress. They describe the court, with its flatterers who surround the king with lies. Adam says that they contain political judgements which already announce the writers of the next century. The Fables are still learned by heart in French schools today. Behind their simple stories is a calm but sad view of power and of what happens to weak people. Nicolas Boileau (1636–1711) was one of the main judges of literary taste in his time. He began with satires. From 1672, he read parts of his Art poétique in the salons, and Madame de Sévigné called it a masterpiece. It was published in July 1674. The poem has four parts and explains the rules of good writing in verse. It was a huge success: ten editions in two years and twenty-nine more before 1697. More than anything else, he asked writers to think clearly. Later readers treated the poem as the law of classicism. However, Adam notes that Boileau knew the history of French poetry badly. Rohou calls the book a collection of received ideas, which ignores Ronsard and refuses the farces of Molière. The novel was not highly respected. Serious readers often saw it as light reading, especially suited to women. However, the form continued to grow. The first important fashion was the pastoral novel. L'Astrée by Honoré d'Urfé began to appear in 1607 and grew to thousands of pages. After the author's death, his secretary continued it in 1627. Its shepherds and shepherdesses talk about love in an ideal countryside that never really existed. D'Urfé himself said that the book told the story of his own youth under the disguise of shepherds. Then came the long heroic novel. Madeleine de Scudéry wrote books in ten volumes, filled with battles, kidnappings, and very long conversations about love and feelings. Other writers made fun of these long novels. In Histoire comique de Francion, Charles Sorel follows a poor young man through taverns and law courts. Sorel also wrote Le Berger extravagant (1627), about a young man who has read too many pastoral novels and thinks that he is a shepherd. In a later edition, he called it an anti-roman, a book written against the usual kind of novel. In Le Roman comique, Paul Scarron tells the story of a travelling group of actors. Antoine Furetière describes middle-class Paris and its legal arguments in Le Roman bourgeois (1666). Cyrano de Bergerac sent his hero to the Moon and the Sun in two stories that mix travel, science, and jokes about religion. Both were printed only after his death, in 1657 and 1662, and the first was cut to remove its attacks on religion. At the same time, a much shorter kind of novel began to appear. Madame de La Fayette had already published La Princesse de Montpensier, a short story set at the same court. It is often seen as a first sketch of her masterpiece. La Princesse de Clèves (1678), by Madame de La Fayette, has only a few main characters and a simple story. A young married woman falls in love with another man. She tells her husband about her feelings, and after her husband dies, she still refuses to marry the man she loves. The book went on sale in the middle of March 1678 without the author's name. Readers guessed that Madame de La Fayette had written it, but she denied it in her letters. Only much later did she admit that her friends La Rochefoucauld and Segrais had helped her a little with corrections. The story is set at the court of Henry II, more than a century earlier. But she said that it was a perfect picture of life at court in her own time. Readers argued about it in print, especially in a newspaper called the Mercure galant. One important question was whether a wife would really confess such feelings to her husband. The novel studies what people feel and why they act as they do. It is often called the first modern French novel. However, this description reflects later ideas about the novel as much as the ideas of 1678. Madame de La Fayette herself did not want her book to be called a roman. For her, a roman meant a long story full of adventures, and she said that her own book was very different from that. Stendhal later placed it above every other novel, and Adam compares its study of love and jealousy to the work of Marcel Proust. Some of the best prose of the 17th century was not fiction. Writers known as moralists carefully watched how people behaved and wrote about what they saw in short texts. The Duc de La Rochefoucauld (1613–1680) wrote the Maximes. A maxim is a very short statement, usually only one or two lines long. He had fought against the king's government during the civil war called the Fronde, and he first wrote his memoirs. Around 1658, he and his friend the Marquise de Sablé began a salon game: each wrote short sentences about human conduct and exchanged them. Two friends helped him, and by the end of 1660 he had copied a whole volume of maxims by hand. In 1664, a pirated edition was printed in Holland, so he published the book himself in Paris. It appeared with the date 1665. He kept changing it, and later editions grew from about 300 to more than 500 maxims. His main subject is self-love. He argues that even when people do something good, they are often thinking about themselves. Jean de La Bruyère (1645–1696) was born in Paris. He was a lawyer, and in 1673 he bought an office in the finances of Normandy, but he went on living in Paris in a modest room. In 1684, Bossuet found him a post as tutor to the grandson of the Prince de Condé. From then on, he lived inside one of the greatest families of the kingdom. His Caractères appeared in March 1688, without his name, as an appendix to his translation of the Greek writer Theophrastus. The book sold so well that two more editions were printed in the same year. He kept adding to it, and the portraits that made it famous only appeared from the fourth edition. Before that, the book was closer to the maxims of La Rochefoucauld. He created short portraits of different kinds of people: the rich fool, the boring man, or the person who is always in a hurry. Madame de Sévigné (1626–1696) was widowed in 1651 and shone in the salons of Paris. She was a friend of La Rochefoucauld and Madame de La Fayette, and she admired Corneille. On 4 February 1671, her daughter left Paris to join her husband, who had been made the king's lieutenant in Provence. Madame de Sévigné wrote that it felt as if her heart was being torn out. In fact, she spent about two thirds of the twenty-five years that remained to her near her daughter, in Paris or in Provence. When they were apart, she wrote to her twice a week, at length, and waited anxiously for every reply. Madame de Sévigné did not write these letters for the public. The first of them were printed in 1697, the year after her death, among the letters of her cousin Bussy-Rabutin. A fuller edition appeared in 1734 and 1737, and in 1784 the family burned the original letters. They are now read as literature. They describe life at court, gossip, illness, and love in a lively and natural style. Adam says that they reflect the whole age of Louis XIV better than the plays of Molière, and that Proust compared her to the Impressionist painters. After 1680, the mood at court changed. Louis XIV became devout and stopped going to the theatre. On 21 October 1680, he had ordered the two Paris companies to join together as the Comédie-Française. Preachers attacked the theatre as a school of the devil, and in 1694 Bossuet, the greatest preacher of the age, published a book that condemned it. Bossuet's funeral speeches were public events. Madame de Sévigné described the crowds that came to see the decorations for his speech on the death of the Prince de Condé in 1687. Comedy did well all the same. Regnard and Dancourt wrote comedies about the manners of the time, and Lesage, who loved Spanish literature, published Le Diable boiteux in 1707. Rohou calls the years from 1682 to about 1706 a period of critical analysis. Two writers of this period prepared the ideas of the 18th century. Fontenelle (1657–1757), a nephew of Corneille, was born in Rouen. His Entretiens sur la pluralité des mondes (1686) explained the new astronomy to a lady during evening walks in a garden. In his Histoire des oracles (1686), he argued that ignorance, respect for tradition, and the interest of priests explain the belief in false miracles. He was careful, and he made an exception for Christianity, but his readers understood the lesson.

German literature is the texts written in the German language. This includes literature written in Germany, Austria, the German parts of Switzerland and Belgium, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, South Tyrol in Italy and also books written by the German diaspora. Italian literature is written in the Italian language, especially in Italy. It may also refer to literature written by Italians or in other languages spoken in Italy, often languages that are very similar to modern Italian, including regional varieties and dialects. Italian literature begins in the 12th century, when in different areas of the peninsula the Italian vernacular started to be used to write books. The Ritmo laurenziano is the first text of Italian literature. One of the first examples of Italian literature is the tradition of lyric poetry sung in Occitan. This tradition arrived in Italy by the end of the 12th century. In 1230, the Sicilian School became famous for being the first style in standard Italian. Dante Alighieri, one of the greatest of Italian poets, is important and famous for being the author of La Divina Commedia (The Divine Comedy, c. 1308–1320). Renaissance humanism developed during the 14th and the beginning of the 15th centuries. Early Italian humanists, such as the lyric poet Francesco Petrarca and the Neoplatonist philosopher Marsilio Ficino, were highly educated Classical scholars and great collectors of old manuscripts. The development of the drama in the 15th century was very great. In the 16th century, the main feature of the time following the end of the Renaissance is that it perfected the Italian character of its language. Niccolò Machiavelli and Francesco Guicciardini were the chief originators of the science of history. Pietro Bembo was an famous and important figure in the development of the Italian language and an influence on the 16th-century renewed interest in the works of Petrarca. In 1690, the Academy of Arcadia was created with the goal of "restoring" literature by copying the simplicity of the old shepherds. In the 18th century, the political condition of the Italian states began to improve, and philosophers spread their writings and ideas throughout Europe during the Age of Enlightenment. Apostolo Zeno and Metastasio are two of the important figures of the age. Carlo Goldoni, a Venetian playwright and librettist, created the comedy of character. The leading figure of the 18th-century Italian literary revival was Giuseppe Parini. The ideas behind the French Revolution of 1789 gave a special direction to Italian literature in the second half of the 18th century. It began with the publication of the book Dei delitti e delle pene (On Crimes and Punishments, 1764) by Cesare Beccaria. Patriotism and classicism were the two ways of thinking that motivated the literature that began with the Italian playwright and poet Vittorio Alfieri. Others include the poets Vincenzo Monti and Ugo Foscolo. The Romantic movement had as its organ the Conciliatore, established in 1818 at Milan. The main initiator of the reform was the Italian poet and author Alessandro Manzoni, known for his historical novel I promessi sposi (The Betrothed, 1827–1842). The great Italian poet of the age was Giacomo Leopardi. The bookish movement that happened before and at the same time as the political revolutions of 1848 was represented by four writers: Giuseppe Giusti, Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi, Vincenzo Gioberti, and Cesare Balbo. After the Risorgimento, political literature became less important. During the first part of this period, two different tendencies of literature against Romanticism appeared: the Scapigliatura and Verismo. The most well-known figure of Verismo was the Sicilian writer Giovanni Verga, author of I Malavoglia (The House by the Medlar-Tree, 1881). Important early 20th-century Italian writers include Giovanni Pascoli, Italo Svevo, Gabriele D'Annunzio, Umberto Saba, Giuseppe Ungaretti, Eugenio Montale, and Luigi Pirandello (winner of the 1934 Nobel Prize in Literature). Neorealism was developed by Alberto Moravia. Umberto Eco became successful with the detective story Il nome della rosa (The Name of the Rose, 1980). Six Italian authors have received the Nobel Prize in Literature. These are Giosuè Carducci, Grazia Deledda, Luigi Pirandello, Salvatore Quasimodo, Eugenio Montale, and Dario Fo.
